title: Spezzatino di manzo
subtitle: Italian braised beef stew with tomato and red wine
excerpt: Spezzatino di manzo is the Italian beef braise: chunks of chuck cooked slowly in red wine and tomato until the meat collapses into tender, falling pieces. It is a simple one-pot dish that rewards at least two hours on a very low flame. Serve it with soft polenta or mashed potato.
sourceNotes: Italian home-cooking tradition. Beef stews braised in wine and tomato are made across Tuscany, Umbria, and Lazio. Method drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Thaw overnight and reheat gently with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the recipe; freeze half in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Better the next day. Make ahead and reheat.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian braised meat stew; the name comes from spezzare, meaning 'to break into pieces'; the meat is cut into chunks and braised slowly until tender.

content.text: Spezzatino di manzo is an Italian

of beef chuck braised in red wine and tomato until the meat is fork-tender. There is very little active work: brown the meat, build the base, cover, and leave it alone for two hours. Use a heavy-based casserole and the lowest heat your hob can manage.

Season {{beef-chuck}} of beef chunks with salt and pepper. Toss lightly in {{plain-flour}} of flour, shaking off the excess. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large casserole over high heat. Brown the beef in batches, about 5 minutes per batch, until dark on all sides. Remove and set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 8 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and cook for 1 minute. Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine, scraping up the pan. Let it reduce by half. Add the tomatoes, {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, {{bay-leaves}} of bay leaves, and the rosemary sprig.

Return the beef to the pot. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover tightly, and cook over the lowest heat for 1.5 to 2 hours until the meat is very tender and the sauce has thickened. Adjust seasoning. Remove the bay leaves and rosemary. Serve with polenta, mashed potato, or crusty bread.

items.symptom: Meat is still tough after 2 hours
items.cause: Heat too high, or beef cut too large.
items.fix: The braise needs a bare simmer, not a boil. Continue cooking; chuck can take up to 2.5 hours.

items.cause: Not cooked uncovered long enough at the end.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final 20 minutes and let the sauce reduce.

content.text: Spezzatino of some kind is eaten across Italy, from the wine-braised Tuscan versions to the tomato-rich southern ones. It is winter food that gets better each time it is reheated. Many Italian home cooks make it on Saturday for Sunday, then again on Monday. Soft polenta is the usual accompaniment in Lombardy and Veneto; further south, thick pasta or mashed potato do the same job.
